title: Trip Distance Per Day Calculator
description: Split a trip's total distance across its travel days with the Trip Distance Per Day Calculator — the daily target your itinerary needs. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 1,850 miles over six travel days is 308 miles a day — a gentle target that leaves afternoons for the places the trip is supposedly for.
quick_answer: The Trip Distance Per Day Calculator divides a journey's total distance by its travel days and returns the distance each day must cover. Enter the route total and your days, and read the daily target — the number telling you whether the itinerary is a holiday or endurance event.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
Distance per day: a trip's total distance divided by its travel days — the daily target the itinerary must deliver.
Do I need an account?
No. Total and days in, daily target out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
For tour and rota planning, yes — it is the budgeting division behind every sane itinerary. Legal driving limits sit on top of it for professionals.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Traffic changes hours, not the distance target; convert your target with your real average speed to feel the day's length.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Enter the road total — days are spent on road miles.
Should rest days count as travel days?
No — divide by driving days only, then place rest days in the calendar as themselves. Hidden rest days are how itineraries quietly break.
Uneven days?
Real trips bunch near sights and spread on transit days. The average here is the budget; the Overnight Stop Planner shapes the actual days.
My days include sightseeing days.
Then divide by travel days only, and let the sights have their own calendar entries — diluted averages lie about both.
The daily target looks fine but the hours do not.
Convert with your real average speed: 308 gentle miles at 40 mph is a longer day than 400 at 65. This page budgets miles; the ETA tools budget the day.
Cycling tour — same thinking?
Identical, at cycling numbers: 40–60 mile days. The division does not care what turns the wheels.
